rows.ideal_execution_standard: The millisecond the eyes locate the post, drive the OUTSIDE cutting foot down into a compact step tightly aligned within the frame. The toe is pulled upward into dorsiflexion right before contact to establish a firm ankle lock. The cleat slams down directly beneath the hips, instantly pointing the toe at a sharp 45-degree angle toward the post.

rows.fault_trigger: FLATTENING THE ROUTE - letting the route drift flat toward the opposite sideline instead of holding a true 45-degree angle toward the goal post, which takes the tight end out of the intended throwing window.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot, snap the hips wide open, and punch the outside arm across the body to accelerate down the 45-degree track, holding a low, aggressive acceleration posture.

rows.fault_trigger: BAILING OFF-TRACK - drifting wide toward the sideline or inside toward the middle right off the snap. Scurrying off the track ruins the spacing of the concept and runs the tight end straight into zone defenders.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the ball with a violent, low pad-level release to clear the press defender's hands and establish a strict linear track down the hashes or the seam lane, then transition smoothly into top-end sprint posture with stride lengths opening to maximum expansion, chin tucked and core locked on the track.

rows.fault_trigger: SLOWING DOWN FOR CONTACT - decelerating or stutter-stepping when an inside linebacker tries to reroute or jam. The tight end must sprint through the contact and use the hands to clear without dropping speed. (Defender contact is not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pushing through the intermediate zone at 10-12 yards, expect a collision or squeeze from interior linebackers or safeties. Use a high-speed hand swipe, chop or arm bar to clear their contact while holding the vertical line without drifting off-track or losing a step.

rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING / FLOPPY FOOTWORK - reaching too far forward to try to outrun a deep safety, or running with a loose, downward-pointing toe. This strips core stability and caps top-end speed. Also: drifting laterally out of the void.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Squeeze tightly into the defensive void with the running track completely straight. Steps stay compact and directly beneath the centre of mass without overstriding, toes pulling up into sharp dorsiflexion on every stride for a rigid ankle lock, while the eyes track the ball over the inside shoulder.

rows.fault_trigger: EXPOSING THE BALL - catching with the body loose or waiting for the ball to hit the chest. Over the middle, failing to snatch with extended hands and instantly tuck results in drops and forced fumbles. (Ball position and contact are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Expect a heavy hit from a closing safety or linebacker over the middle. Keep the hands down late to mask the ball's arrival, then shoot the arms up violently to snap the ball out of the air at its highest point, instantly tucking it to protect against incoming contact.

rows.fault_trigger: BANANA STEMMING - curving the path inward before the actual break, letting an inside-shade defender stay in front the whole way. CHOPPING FEET - gathering or stutter-stepping before the break; a slant relies entirely on pure unmitigated speed, and chopping ruins the separation.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Fire off the line hard for 3 direct vertical strides in a fierce sprint-sell posture - the path must look identical to a go route to freeze the defender's feet and leverage. On the second step, subtly drop the hips an inch into a compact athletic posture while the feet keep moving at full velocity.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with or after the plant rather than leading it, so the tight end breaks across the defender's face without having cleared his vision - and on a route this quick, the ball is often already out. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At the exact peak of the third stride, snap the head and eyes inside across the middle of the field first. The visual snap instantly clears vision to read the inside linebackers and pick up the ball's release.

rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING THE BREAK - reaching too far inside with a long, diving step. This elongates the body frame, tells the defender exactly when the break is coming, and locks up the hips so the tight end cannot accelerate smoothly out of the cut.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The split-second the eyes turn, drive the outside foot down into a controlled step tightly aligned within the frame. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion before impact to establish a firm ankle lock, and the step is not overextended. The cleat slams down directly beneath the hips, instantly directing the toe at a sharp 45 degrees toward the middle to slice across the defender's face without losing linear body control.

rows.fault_trigger: RUNNING FLAT - flattening the route out horizontally toward the opposite sideline. The tight end must hold a strict 45-degree angle to keep outrunning the trailing defender. (Ball location needs ball tracking.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Roll the body weight smoothly off the directing foot, punch the outside arm violently across the body to hold top sprinting speed, maintain the 45-degree trajectory, and catch the ball cleanly in stride.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotated away from the line before the snap, telegraphing the release direction to the defender, or shoulder line unlevel enough to unbalance the first step.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Shoulders remain controlled and aligned with the intended release position. The upper body should not rotate excessively away from the line before movement begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Front knee locked or straight, knee collapsing inside or outside the toe line, or rear knee too extended to contribute to the first movement.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Front knee is bent rather than locked. The knee tracks forward toward the toe while maintaining an athletic loaded position. Rear knee remains flexed enough to contribute to the first movement.

rows.fault_trigger: Outside foot forward instead of the inside foot; stagger too deep or too shallow to release cleanly; front toe square or turned outward rather than slightly in; or the inward turn overdone so it pulls the hips inside and opens them before the snap. (Which foot is 'inside' depends on alignment side - not determinable from a solo clip.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Inside foot is forward, toward the ball. Feet maintain the appropriate stagger and orientation to allow the tight end to release without a false step. The front foot carries a very slight inward turn - enough to aid the release, but not so much that the turn carries up into the hips and opens them inside. The front foot supports the initial roll-off movement.

rows.fault_trigger: Base too narrow to balance, or so wide it restricts the first step and forces a false step to recover.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Feet are approximately shoulder width apart, providing a stable and explosive base. The stance is wide enough for balance without restricting the first step.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands crossed over the body's midline, clamped tight to the torso, or held so low or high that the tight end cannot react to a press. Arms rigid rather than relaxed. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hands remain relaxed, uncrossed, and independent. Hands are positioned near the waist or slightly higher in front of the chest depending on anticipated coverage. Hands remain free to immediately react to a press defender.

rows.fault_trigger: Standing too tall with no forward readiness, or crouching so low the tight end cannot release cleanly. Chest behind or well past the front knee.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Chest and hips are lowered into an athletic position. The shoulders/chest are positioned over the front knee, creating forward readiness without excessive crouching.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips opened toward the release before movement begins, giving away direction, or hips drifting out from under the torso so the drive is weakened.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hips remain loaded underneath the torso and prepared to drive toward the release. Hips should not be excessively opened before movement begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Torso angle diverging from the shin angle - typically folding forward at the waist with the chest well ahead of the shin line, or standing the torso upright while the shin stays loaded, disconnecting upper and lower body.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Upper body is positioned at approximately the same forward angle as the loaded front shin, creating a connected lower- and upper-body position. Avoid excessive bending at the waist.

rows.fault_trigger: Head facing straight downfield rather than turned inside to the ball, or head unstable/bobbing pre-snap so the tight end reacts late. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only. Ball location needs ball tracking.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Head is turned inside toward the football before the snap, with eyes locked onto the ball. The tight end uses the football's movement as the visual snap cue rather than reacting to the quarterback's verbal cadence. Head position remains controlled and stable so the tight end can explode immediately when the ball is snapped without a false start.

rows.fault_trigger: Swaying, rocking, or bouncing pre-snap rather than settling into a loaded position; or so rigid and locked that the first movement requires a reset. A false step at the snap is the downstream symptom.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Tight end remains stable but immediately movable. The stance is sufficiently loaded to prevent a false step while allowing explosive movement in the intended release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Weight sitting back on the rear leg or evenly split, forcing a backward rock or false step before the release.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Approximately 70-80% of body weight is loaded onto the front leg. The rear leg remains available to contribute to the release. The tight end should be able to roll forward off the front foot without rocking backward or taking a false step.

rows.fault_trigger: "The Double-Clutch". Attempting to make a dynamic football move or turn up-field before the ball is completely secured in the hands, leading to direct drops or immediate bobble-fumbles upon first contact.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Instantly secure the catch in space and transition the ball directly to the body, completely avoiding any "double-clutch" or premature up-field turn before the ball is possessed.

rows.fault_trigger: "Flagging" the Ball. Carrying the ball loosely away from the body while running in space. This heavily exposes the ball to trailing defenders punching or stripping it from behind.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hook the fingers over the front point, press the forearm along the seam, and clamp the back half of the football securely between the forearm and bicep.

rows.fault_trigger: Exposing the Breast. Carrying the football across the middle of the chest with a nose-up orientation. This allows a defender to punch it cleanly and violently out from the front.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Press the inner side of the football firmly against the rib cage with the nose tucked up beneath the armpit, completely locking the elbow to the torso to eliminate daylight.
Read interior pursuit and transfer the ball to the outside arm (closest to the sideline), freeing the inside arm to stiff-arm or guard against incoming tacklers.
The moment traffic closes in or a tackle is initiated, wrap the off-hand over the ball (two-handed carry) and chin the football to protect it completely through the ground.

rows.fault_trigger: REACHING WITH ONE HAND - extending only the leading arm, cutting the catching surface in half. Also: the hips rotating with the chest, which breaks the running line and costs stride. (Hand shape needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hold the running trajectory and snap the eyes toward the incoming ball, judging its lateral path while keeping stride length intact. Fire BOTH arms outward away from the torso into the lateral lane, torquing the upper chest slightly toward the ball without breaking the lower body's running line, and form a tight diamond out wide with thumbs and index fingers connected and palms squared to the side-angle trajectory.

rows.fault_trigger: THE PERIPHERAL PEEK - trying to catch using only peripheral vision with the nose pointed straight downfield, which ruins hand-eye coordination and depth perception. THE STIFF LATERAL LOCKOUT - catching out wide with locked elbows, so the ball clanks off rigid fingertips.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Intercept the nose of the ball out wide in the centre of the diamond, elbows unlocked to absorb the high-velocity lateral momentum. The nose must be pointed exactly at the hands at the moment of impact - not tracking the ball peripherally.

rows.fault_trigger: The head snapping back downfield while the ball is still being swept across the body, so the rotational momentum of the sweep pulls the eyes off the leather and the ball is lost mid-transfer.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Sweep the ball back tightly across the body into the core ribcage, instantly snapping the chin down and across the torso to visually lock the ball into the tuck position before looking upfield.

rows.fault_trigger: TURNING PINKIES UP - reaching up and out with the pinkies together, which turns the palms completely away from the ball's path. THE OVERHEAD CLAP - slapping the hands together laterally from the sides instead of clamping the ball's incoming line. (Hand orientation needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Track the high, fading trajectory and time the jump or upper-body extension to meet the ball out wide at its highest point. Shoot both arms violently upward and outward on a 45-degree diagonal with elbows slightly flexed, hands open wide with thumbs locked together and index fingers pointing diagonally upward to form the overhead triangle.

rows.fault_trigger: THE EARLY CENTRE DROP - catching the ball diagonally but snapping the head back to the centre of the field before pulling it down, leading to a blind tuck and a high chance of dropping it on turf impact.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pluck the ball out of the air at its highest possible lateral apex, staring directly through the diagonal window formed by the hands. The head must not drift back toward the centre of the body before the ball is secured.

rows.fault_trigger: The head returning to centre or upfield before the ball reaches the chest, completing the tuck blind - the most common way a spectacular high-and-wide catch becomes a drop on landing.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pull the ball down violently across the chest, rolling the head diagonally downward to visually track the ball all the way from the high-outside quadrant into chest protection as the feet return to the turf.

rows.fault_trigger: WAIST-BENDING REACHES - keeping the legs straight and bending sideways at the waist, which destroys balance and pulls the eyes away from the ball. THUMBS-TOGETHER LOW CATCH - trying to scoop a low-lateral ball with the thumbs together, forcing the palms to face the ground. (Hand inversion needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Track the low, diving path and drop the entire body level by bending deeply at the knees and hips. Drop both arms diagonally downward toward the grass on the catch side with elbows tucked near the lower ribcage, inverting the hands out to the side - pinky fingers pressed tightly together, palms facing upward and outward - to form a secure under-scoop.

rows.fault_trigger: Eyes lifting off the basket before the fingers close. On a low-and-wide catch the hands are at their furthest from the head, so peripheral tracking is at its least reliable and the margin is smallest.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Slide the inverted hands underneath the dipping path of the ball, with the chin tucked to the catch-side shoulder and the eyes glued to the grass-level pinky basket as the ball settles in.

rows.fault_trigger: THE UP-AND-OUT PULL - catching the ball low and wide but immediately pulling the head up and away to look at a defender, so the ball slips out of the pinkies during the lateral sweep. The longest, least secure transfer of any catch in the set.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Roll the hands and forearms upward and across the stomach, keeping the head down and rotated laterally. Watch the ball leave the lateral plane and physically touch the stomach before the eyes snap up to run.

rows.fault_trigger: BODY CATCHING - letting the ball travel all the way into the chest pads instead of extending the hands, so it bounces off hard plastic armour and results in drops or deflections. (Hand shape needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hold a strong base with the eyes locked on the point of the ball. Shoot the arms forward away from the jersey to meet the ball early and maximise the catching radius, forming a tight symmetric diamond with thumbs and index fingers pressed together and palms turned outward to face the incoming ball.

rows.fault_trigger: THE EARLY LOOK - snapping the head up to look at an oncoming defender right before the ball hits the hands, causing a ricochet off the fingertips. THE STIFF-ARM CLANK - catching with locked-out elbows and hard palms; without joint elasticity a fast ball clanks off the hands. (Ball contact needs object detection.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Let the nose of the ball enter the centre of the diamond while the eyes stay hyper-focused on the leather. The elbows stay relaxed and flexible to give with the ball and absorb its force, with the fingertips - not the palms - clamping the panels.

rows.fault_trigger: Eyes leaving the ball before the tuck is complete - the head comes up to find defenders while the ball is still being secured, which is how a clean catch becomes a fumble. Also: no chin drop at all, so the catch is never visually confirmed.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pull the ball tightly back into the ribcage, wrapping the arm completely over it for a four-point pressure hold. Instantly drop the chin to visually confirm the catch - nose to the tuck - before snapping the eyes upfield to look for defenders.

rows.fault_trigger: TURNING PINKIES OUT - reaching up for a high ball with the pinkies together instead of the thumbs. This turns the palms away from the ball and makes a clean high catch impossible. (Hand orientation needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Track the high trajectory and time the jump or extension so the hands intercept the ball at the absolute apex of reach. Shoot both arms violently upward above the forehead with elbows slightly flexed, hands open wide with thumbs pressed tightly together and index fingers pointing up, creating an inverted triangle to look through.

rows.fault_trigger: THE BLIND PULL - tilting the head back down toward the turf before the hands secure the ball, resulting in a blind, clapping attempt at the apex. CLAPPING AT THE BALL - slapping the hands together from the sides; if the timing is off by a millisecond the palms hit the ball and knock it away.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stare directly through the window created by the hands and pluck the ball out of the air at its highest possible point, fingers spread wide and thumbs facing each other right before impact, fingertips wrapping tightly around the tip and sides to halt its momentum mid-air.

rows.fault_trigger: Head staying tilted up after the catch rather than following the ball down into the body, so the tuck is never visually confirmed. Also: landing stiff-legged without knee flexion, costing balance and the ability to run after the catch.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pull the ball down violently to the chest as the feet return to the turf, the head snapping down to follow the ball's descent from the sky straight into the core, then immediately roll the body or shoulders over the ball to protect it from closing defenders.

rows.fault_trigger: BENDING AT THE WAIST - keeping the legs straight and simply leaning over. This ruins balance, alters eye level dramatically, and prevents running after the catch. THUMBS-UP MISTAKE - trying to catch a low ball with the thumbs together like a chest catch, forcing the hands upside down so the ball slips straight through onto the ground. (Hand inversion needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Track the downward trajectory and lower the entire body frame by bending at the knees and hips rather than folding at the waist. Drop the arms toward the grass with elbows tucked close to the torso, then invert the hands completely - pinky fingers pressed together, palms facing upward - creating a clean scoop to cradle the dipping ball.

rows.fault_trigger: EARLY EYES - snapping the head up to look at the defence while the ball is still inches from the pinkies, causing it to slip through the arms onto the grass. On a low catch there is no margin: the eyes must stay down until the fingers close.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Keep the eyes hyper-focused on the hands and slide the inverted basket underneath the path of the ball, fingertips angled slightly upward right before impact, letting the ball land smoothly into the pinky basket while the fingers instantly curl around the leather.

rows.fault_trigger: Looking up to run before the ball is rolled securely into the abdomen. The low catch is the least secure of all four, so any early upfield glance during the roll-up is how the ball ends up on the grass.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Roll the hands and forearms upward toward the stomach, cradling the ball securely against the body frame so it cannot slip out. The eyes stay locked on the ball as it transitions from the grass line up into the stomach - do not look up to run yet.

rows.fault_trigger: REACHING EARLY - running downfield with the arms extended to the sky for ten yards. This alerts the defender to play the arms, slows top sprint speed, and makes tracking the ball far harder. (Basket formation needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Sprint at top speed along the route track with a steady, bounce-free head. Keep the hands down and relaxed while running, extending the arms upward only at the absolute last second to keep the trailing defender blind, then raise the hands near collarbone or chin level with pinkies pressed together and palms open to the sky, forming a deep running basket.

rows.fault_trigger: PEEKING - letting the head drift back forward toward the end zone just before the ball drops into the bucket, so it hits the helmet or falls straight through the hands. THE PALMS-FORWARD BARRIER - facing the palms toward the line of scrimmage instead of up to the sky, creating a wall the ball bounces off rather than a basket it falls into.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The eyes track the nose of the ball dropping from the sky straight down into the open palms. The wrists stay completely loose and cushioned right before impact, letting the ball melt into the fingers without disrupting the running stride.

rows.fault_trigger: Snapping the head forward before the ball is secured into the chest pocket, so the catch is completed blind. Also: breaking stride or stuttering during the tuck, which surrenders the separation the route created.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Clamp the fingers around the ball the instant it settles into the hands, pulling it straight down into the pocket arm position while the head stays rotated over the shoulder and the eyes stay locked on the hands until the ball is safely into the chest - all without breaking the vertical sprint into the end zone.

rows.fault_trigger: Standing straight up out of the stance, killing acceleration; or bending at the waist so the chest folds forward ahead of the hips instead of the whole body leaning.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso leans forward through the initial acceleration, driving the body out of the stance. The lean comes from the whole body angled forward, not from bending at the waist.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders spiking upright on the first step rather than rising gradually, losing the forward drive angle and slowing acceleration.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pads stay low out of the stance and rise gradually across the first steps as speed builds, rather than popping upright immediately.

rows.fault_trigger: Long ground contact times, or the foot striking ahead of the body with backward velocity - braking on each step instead of driving.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Ground contact is short and driving - the foot strikes underneath the body and leaves quickly, adding speed rather than absorbing it.

rows.fault_trigger: First step drifting laterally off the release heading, widening the path and costing ground before the route develops.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first step travels directly along the intended release heading, without lateral drift that costs ground or telegraphs the release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Base widening through the first steps, costing efficiency and drive; or narrowing so far the receiver crosses over and loses balance.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Feet stay under the body through the first steps - narrow enough to run efficiently, wide enough to stay balanced through the acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms out of sync with the legs, arms crossing the body's midline rather than driving forward and back, or elbows flailing/locking so the arms add no drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Arms drive in rhythm with the legs - opposite arm to opposite leg - with the elbows held at a consistent working angle to add drive out of the stance.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating away from the hips and the release path, disconnecting upper and lower body and telegraphing the release direction.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Shoulders stay connected to the hips and square to the release path, moving with the lower body rather than rotating independently of it.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips over-rotating off the release heading, widening the path and costing ground; or staying square when the release requires them to turn.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hips stay driving toward the release heading through the first steps, opening only as far as the release path requires.

rows.fault_trigger: Weight stalling or moving backward relative to the feet, so a step catches the body instead of driving it forward.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Weight moves continuously forward through the first three steps, staying ahead of the base of support so each step drives rather than catches.

rows.fault_trigger: Head whipping round or dropping during the release, or failing to transition from the ball to the release path. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Head transitions from the inside snap cue to the release path and defensive target, turning under control without whipping or dropping.

rows.fault_trigger: A false step - a backward or sideways step before the first forward step - losing ground and time before the route begins.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first movement travels forward along the release heading. No backward or lateral step is taken before the release begins - the receiver goes directly from the loaded stance into the first step.

rows.fault_trigger: Overstriding on the first step so the foot lands ahead of the body's mass and brakes rather than drives; or a step so short it fails to create separation.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first step is short and driving rather than long and reaching - it establishes ground contact quickly and underneath the body so the second step can build speed.

rows.fault_trigger: Drifting or rounding off the line rather than committing to a release angle. (Whether the angle matches the called release needs the route to be declared - not determinable from a solo clip.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The body travels on a consistent, committed path off the line, matching the angle the called release requires - inside or outside - without drifting or rounding.

rows.fault_trigger: Backward weight transfer before the roll-off, the whole foot leaving the ground flat rather than rolling through the toe, or excessive vertical rise instead of forward drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver rolls off the front foot into the release - the heel lifts while the toe stays in contact, driving the body forward. The roll-off leads the forward travel rather than following it.

rows.fault_trigger: Weight stalling or falling back behind the feet at any point in the 5 yards, so a step catches the body instead of driving it forward.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Weight moves continuously forward across the full 5 yards, staying ahead of the base of support so every step drives rather than catches.

rows.fault_trigger: Base staying wide through the whole 5 yards, costing efficiency and speed; or narrowing too early so the driving steps lose their power base.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The base starts wider through the driving first steps, then narrows progressively into a linear running track by the fifth yard as the receiver transitions from acceleration to running.

rows.fault_trigger: Head bobbing, whipping or dropping through the drive, so the receiver cannot process the defender's leverage. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation and stability only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays stable and level through the 5-yard drive, held steady enough to read the defender's leverage and cushion while the body accelerates.

rows.fault_trigger: Foot landing ahead of the hips at strike, creating a braking force that costs speed on every step - typically caused by overstriding out of the stance.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Each foot lands under or slightly behind the hips during the acceleration steps, so every strike drives the body forward instead of braking it.

rows.fault_trigger: Backward weight transfer before the roll-off, the whole foot leaving the ground flat rather than rolling through the toe, or excessive vertical rise instead of forward drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver rolls off the front foot into the drive - the heel lifts while the toe stays in contact, driving the body forward. The roll-off leads the forward travel rather than following it.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms out of sync with the legs, swinging across the body's midline rather than driving front-to-back, or elbows flailing and locking so the arms add no drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Arms drive front-to-back in rhythm with the legs - opposite arm to opposite leg - at a consistent elbow angle, without swinging across the body.

rows.fault_trigger: Velocity plateauing early in the 5 yards, or stalling between steps - the receiver reaches a speed and stops building rather than accelerating through the stem. (Absolute rate needs a scale reference.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Speed builds continuously across the first 5 yards - each step adds velocity, with no early plateau or stall in the acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: Excessive torso rotation during max-effort strides - the shoulders counter-rotating hard against the hips, wasting energy that should go into forward drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso stays quiet through the acceleration - shoulders and hips rotate only as much as the stride requires, so energy goes into forward drive rather than twisting.

rows.fault_trigger: A false step - a backward or sideways step before the first forward step - losing ground and time before the stem begins.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first movement travels forward along the release heading. No backward or lateral step is taken before the drive begins - the receiver goes directly from the loaded stance into the first step.

rows.fault_trigger: First step drifting laterally off the release heading, widening the path and costing ground before the route develops.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first step travels directly along the intended release heading, without lateral drift that costs ground or telegraphs the release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Popping upright prematurely rather than rising gradually, losing the forward drive angle and cutting acceleration short.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pads stay low out of the stance and rise smoothly and gradually across the 5 yards as speed builds, reaching upright running posture only once the acceleration phase is complete.

rows.fault_trigger: Strides not expanding - staying short and choppy through the whole 5 yards; or opening up too early, overstriding out of the stance before speed supports it.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length expands progressively across the first 5 yards - short and driving at Step 1, opening up as speed builds through Steps 4 and 5.

rows.fault_trigger: Ground contact times staying flat or lengthening across the 5 yards - the receiver is not converting drive into speed, and each step absorbs rather than adds velocity.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Ground contact shortens progressively across the 5 yards - longer on the driving first steps, then quicker as speed builds and the receiver transitions to running.

rows.fault_trigger: Drifting laterally off the stem heading across the 5 yards, changing the depth and angle at which the break occurs. (Whether the heading matches the called route needs the route to be declared.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The stem holds a straight, committed line across the 5 yards - the body travels on the intended heading without drifting laterally, so the route develops on time and the break happens where it should.

rows.fault_trigger: Standing too upright out of the stance, killing the drive angle; bending at the waist so the chest folds ahead of the hips; or holding the forward angle too long and failing to transition upfield.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds an aggressive forward drive angle through the early steps - roughly 45 to 60 degrees from vertical - then transitions smoothly upfield as speed builds. The angle comes from the whole body driving forward, not from bending at the waist.

rows.fault_trigger: Overstriding on the first step so the foot lands ahead of the body's mass and brakes rather than drives; or a step so short it fails to create separation.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first step is short and driving rather than long and reaching - it establishes ground contact quickly and underneath the body so the following steps can expand.

rows.fault_trigger: Base narrowing into a normal running stride as the receiver closes, so he arrives with no lateral leverage and gets moved off the block on contact.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The base stays wide throughout the approach - noticeably wider than a running stride - so the receiver keeps blocking leverage and can react laterally to the defender.

rows.fault_trigger: Drifting off the tracking line during the approach, so the defender slips past inside or outside before contact is made. (Alignment to the defender needs them in frame - path consistency only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver tracks a consistent line onto the defender, staying square to them so they cannot slip past inside or outside before the hands fit.

rows.fault_trigger: Over-running the block - arriving at full speed with no gather, so the receiver loses balance on contact and the defender sheds him easily. (Cushion distance needs the defender in frame.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver closes the cushion under control - accelerating to eat up ground, then gathering before contact rather than running through the block at full speed.

rows.fault_trigger: Arriving tall and only sinking at or after contact, so the defender gets underneath the receiver's pads and uprights him immediately.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop into a loaded athletic squat before contact, establishing low leverage so the receiver arrives underneath the defender rather than upright.

rows.fault_trigger: Overstriding on the first step so the foot lands ahead of the body's mass, which kills the power base and leaves the receiver reaching rather than driving.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The first step is short, controlled and punchy, planting underneath the body's mass so power is available immediately rather than reaching out and losing the base.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands landing without hip extension behind them - an arms-only block with no ground force, which the defender sheds easily. Or the hips firing before the hands arrive, wasting the drive.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips extend hard as the hands make contact, driving ground force up through the torso and into the defender so the block has power behind it rather than just reach.

rows.fault_trigger: Slow or short hand extension, so the receiver makes contact with his chest rather than his hands and has no control of the defender. (Hand placement on the defender needs them in frame; grip needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands shoot forward violently at engagement, extending fast into the defender's chest frame rather than arriving late or short.

rows.fault_trigger: Engaging with pads high or the torso upright, letting the defender get underneath and upright the receiver, who then loses the block immediately. (Relative pad level needs the defender in frame.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At engagement the shoulders stay low - at or below the defender's pad level - with the torso angled forward so the receiver wins the leverage battle rather than being stood up.

rows.fault_trigger: Arriving on long strides rather than chopping the feet down, leaving the receiver committed and unable to adjust when the defender moves.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The final two steps before contact shorten and quicken, keeping the feet under the body so the receiver can react instantly if the defender moves laterally.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees straightening into contact, leaving the receiver stiff-legged with nothing to absorb the collision or drive through it; or collapsing so deep he cannot move his feet.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The knees hold a strong power angle - roughly 90 to 120 degrees - approaching and through impact, absorbing the collision and providing the platform to drive.

rows.fault_trigger: Dipping or ducking the head before contact - the receiver loses sight of the target and cannot adjust, and it is an unsafe way to take a collision. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays up with the eyes on the target through contact - the receiver sees what he is blocking rather than ducking his head into the collision.

rows.fault_trigger: Stopping the feet on contact and leaning on the defender, or standing up and narrowing the base after the hit - either way the block is lost within a second.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The feet keep driving after contact, moving the defender while the base stays wide and the knees stay bent - the block is sustained rather than a single hit.

rows.fault_trigger: Passive or low-amplitude arm action that does not match a real sprint, leaving the upper body out of step with the feet and weakening the fake.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump hard at chest height in a genuine sprint-start rhythm, matching what a real slant release would look like.

rows.fault_trigger: Drive leg too straight at push-off, producing little ground force, so the attack step lacks the urgency needed to make the fake believable.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The drive leg holds an acute bend - roughly 110 to 130 degrees - producing maximum ground force to launch onto the diagonal.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders lagging behind the feet or staying upright rather than driving low onto the diagonal, so the upper body never commits to the lie.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders rotate fully square to the 45 degree line with the torso driving low and forward, exactly as they would on a genuine slant.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying square while only the feet take the diagonal, so the fake is not sold and a disciplined defender reads the outside release immediately.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips accelerate along the 45 degree path and rotate fully onto the inside diagonal, committing the whole body to the fake from the first step.

rows.fault_trigger: LOOKING AT THE DEFENDER - peeking at the DB instead of locking down the 45 degree track, which breaks the illusion before it is established. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head locks straight down the 45 degree inside path from the first step, selling the route rather than checking on the defender.

rows.fault_trigger: SOFT FIRST STEP - taking a tentative, short step instead of an aggressive 45 degree launch. The receiver must look like he is sprinting a slant from step one. Also: losing ground backward before the step fires.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The back foot fires outward on a sharp 45 degree diagonal toward the inside lane, launching straight onto the diagonal track with no ground given up first.

rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the push step, which tips that a plant is coming rather than a continued sprint inside.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso stays low and forward in an aggressive sprinting posture through the push step, matching what a genuine slant would look like.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising through the push step, so the receiver looks like he is preparing to stop rather than sprinting a route - the defender reads the cut coming.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay dropped and fully committed to the inside trajectory, holding the low sprinting position that makes the fake believable.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive on the push step, betraying that the receiver is not truly accelerating and is already preparing to plant.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The back knee drives high and hard on the push step, simulating full sprint acceleration so nothing about the movement suggests a fake.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning back toward the outside before the plant, breaking the deception early and letting the defender sit on the breakout. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked straight down the inside path through the push step, holding the deception right up until the plant.

rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump dropping off during the push step, which signals to the defender that the receiver is about to stop rather than continuing inside.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arm pump continues at full amplitude through the push step, sustaining the impression of a slant or post being run at full effort.

rows.fault_trigger: The second step drifting off the 45 degree line or shortening, so the diagonal track bends and the defender reads that the inside move is not real.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The opposite foot drives down the exact same 45 degree line as the first step, taking real ground inside so the fake reads as a committed route.

rows.fault_trigger: The plant foot sliding or drifting at contact rather than gripping, so the momentum is not arrested and the receiver needs extra steps to change direction.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: On the third step the outside foot slams into the turf along the 45 degree line and grips, acting as a violent brake that kills the inside momentum in one contact.

rows.fault_trigger: Head starting to turn back outside before the plant lands, giving the defender an early warning and letting them jump the breakout. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head holds the inside fake alignment right up to the exact plant frame, then prepares to snap back - the deception is maintained to the last possible instant.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying wide or low at the plant, leaving the chest unprotected at the exact moment a defender who bought the fake is arriving. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside hand crosses over the chest frame at the plant, shielding the body against any late contact from a defender closing on the fake.

rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff, straight leg, which cannot absorb the momentum or store energy - the receiver slides through the cut and the breakout has no power.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee flexes deep - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - creating a spring-loaded platform to drive back out toward the sideline.

rows.fault_trigger: POP-UP BRAKING - letting the chest and hips rise when trying to stop. Without sinking the hips to absorb the momentum, the receiver slides or stumbles instead of cutting cleanly.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop sharply and shift slightly back at the plant, sinking to absorb the forward momentum and load the push back outside.

rows.fault_trigger: Chest rising or the shoulders falling behind the plant foot, so the weight sits back and the receiver cannot push cleanly back to the outside.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay over the toes as the plant foot lands, keeping the body stacked over the brake and ready to snap back toward the outside.

rows.fault_trigger: No hand action at the breakout, or an arm path that never crosses the shoulder line, leaving a recovering defender's hands attached through the escape. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm executes a heavy downward chop past the shoulder line, clearing the defender's arms as the receiver breaks back to the outside.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the breakout, so the first strides are short and the receiver takes too long to convert the cut into separation.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high toward the sideline and upfield, taking immediate ground and building instant separation out of the cut.

rows.fault_trigger: LEAVING THE CHEST EXPOSED - turning back outside with the chest wide open, which invites a trailing defender to land a heavy recovery punch and push the receiver off his path.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away from the defender as the receiver breaks out, turning the chest off them and eliminating the jersey surface they could grab.

rows.fault_trigger: A rounded or gradual change of direction rather than a sharp reversal, so the diamond flattens into a curve and the defender recovers the ground the fake bought.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant foot drives explosively back toward the outside, the step reversing direction sharply enough to complete the diamond path and escape into the open lane.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening slowly or only partway, so the receiver drifts out of the cut rather than exploding, and the separation the fake created is given straight back.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips snap violently open toward the sideline, flipping the body off the inside track and onto the outside release in one decisive rotation.

rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round slowly after the breakout, so the receiver is late finding the quarterback and the ball on a route designed to come out quickly. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps round toward the sideline and upfield the instant the breakout fires, re-establishing vision to locate the quarterback and track the football.

rows.fault_trigger: Head dipping toward the feet or lifting off the defender's midsection line during the kickstep. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable, and the defender is not in frame - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked forward toward the defender's belt line - reading the hips rather than the hands or the feet.

rows.fault_trigger: Front knee straightening or losing its bend during the kickstep, so no energy is stored and the escape has to be generated from a standing start.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front knee holds an acute bend - roughly 100 to 120 degrees - absorbing force and storing elastic energy for the escape rather than straightening under the load.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating open during the kickstep and telegraphing the release, or the torso leaning back away from the defender instead of staying over the toes.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds a slight forward lean over the toes while the shoulders stay square to the defender, giving away nothing about the intended release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the kickstep, unloading the legs and costing the elastic energy needed to escape.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hips stay sunk low through the kickstep, holding the loaded height established in the stance with no upward rise.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping below the hips during the kickstep, leaving the receiver unable to counter the jam. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hands stay active and up around lower chest height, ready to fight the defender's hands, never dropping below the hips.

rows.fault_trigger: Stepping backward and losing ground to the defender, or kicking the rear foot wide of the front foot rather than directly behind it, which widens the base and slows the escape.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The rear foot kicks directly behind the front foot to load the release, without giving up ground backward. The step loads the body rather than retreating from the line.

rows.fault_trigger: Planting with a braking action that kills momentum, or a base widening beyond shoulder width so the receiver has to gather before escaping.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front foot plants firmly with no braking, and the feet stay tight within the body's frame - at or inside shoulder width - so the escape can fire in either direction.

rows.fault_trigger: A shoulder drifting outside the knee line at the plant, widening the frame and telegraphing the release direction before the crossover begins.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay tucked inside the width of the knees, keeping the frame compact so the defender cannot read which way the release is going.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands hanging away from the frame or extended early, giving the defender something to grab and leaving nothing loaded for the escape. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands retract tight to the lower chest and ribcage in a compact ready position, loaded to swipe or punch as the escape begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying at their kickstep angle or straightening at the plant, so the receiver is upright and committed rather than loaded and able to go either way.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees bend deeper at the plant, dropping the receiver into a loaded crouch that can launch in any direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying high or drifting forward past the plant foot, so the spring never loads and the escape has no power behind it.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop and shift slightly back over the plant foot, compressing like a spring so the escape can launch in any direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Head dipping toward the feet as the body loads at the plant, losing sight of the defender at the moment the release is about to start. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level through the plant, holding a neutral forward line rather than dropping to look at the feet as the body loads.

rows.fault_trigger: Lead knee staying square or trailing the foot across, so the lower body does not commit and the fake reads as a feint rather than a release.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee flexes and drives aggressively inward across the body, pointing along the inside fake path to sell the release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying passive during the crossover, or pumping late so the upper body lags the feet and the fake looks manufactured. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump hard toward the inside lane in time with the crossover step, mimicking a genuine release so the fake is complete from feet to hands.

rows.fault_trigger: A lazy crossover that never clears the midline, or one too slow to be believed - the defender does not bite and the outside lane never opens.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The push off the plant foot drives the rear foot sharply across the body's midline into the inside lane, committing hard enough to sell the inside release.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying level through the crossover, so the upper body never sells the inside move and the defender stays square to the outside release.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder dips hard and the torso leans into the inside lane, committing the upper body to the fake so the defender has to honour it.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying square while only the feet cross over - the fake is not sold, and the defender reads the outside release immediately.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drive hard laterally across the defender's face, rotating toward the inside lane so the whole body sells the fake rather than just the feet.

rows.fault_trigger: Head staying still or turning too slowly during the crossover, leaving the fake incomplete. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps sharply toward the inside lane in time with the crossover, adding the final piece of the fake - the defender reads the eyes as well as the feet.

rows.fault_trigger: Running through the release square-shouldered, presenting a full chest for the defender to get hands on and re-route the receiver.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away from the defender - getting skinny - so the receiver presents the narrowest possible surface as he clears the contact window.

rows.fault_trigger: Head staying turned toward the fake after the escape, or turning back slowly, so the receiver loses track of the defender and is late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps back upfield to align with the route, re-establishing vision quickly so the receiver can track the cushion and find the ball.

rows.fault_trigger: A gather step or hesitation between the crossover and the burst, giving the defender time to recover and closing the outside lane the fake just opened.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The crossover foot plants and immediately pushes off into the outside lane - no gather step, no pause. The redirect is instantaneous, converting the fake straight into the escape.

rows.fault_trigger: No hand action at the escape, or an arm path that never clears the shoulder plane, leaving the defender's hands attached through the release. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives sharply past the shoulder plane - swipe, chop or swim - clearing the defender's hands as the body escapes outside.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating slowly or incompletely, so the receiver drifts sideways out of the release instead of driving upfield, losing ground on the route stem.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate sharply from the inside fake toward the sideline and upfield, converting the lateral momentum of the crossover into vertical drive up the field.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive and an incomplete trailing-leg extension, so the first strides out of the release are short and the receiver takes too long to reach full speed.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high and the trailing leg extends fully at push-off, taking ground upfield immediately rather than shuffling out of the release.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the slide, which pops the body upward into a hop; or collapsing so deep the receiver cannot cover ground laterally.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees hold a consistent bend - roughly 120 to 140 degrees - through the slide, producing a smooth lateral glide with no upward bounce.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating away from the hips during the slide, disconnecting the upper body and signalling the release direction before the receiver has committed.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay wide, level and square to the defender, moving with the hips rather than rotating independently of them.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating during the slide, opening the receiver to the defender and tipping the release; or the hips rising and falling, which turns a glide into a hop.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips travel horizontally at a constant height with no rotation, staying square to the defender so the slide gives away nothing about the eventual release.

rows.fault_trigger: Head dropping to watch the feet during the slide, or turning upfield early and telegraphing the vertical release. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked on the defender's belt line throughout the slide, tracking them laterally without dropping to the feet.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping as the receiver concentrates on the footwork, leaving him with no answer if the defender reaches out mid-slide. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay up at lower chest height and relaxed through the slide, ready to react the instant a jam comes.

rows.fault_trigger: THE BUNNY HOP - jumping or leaping sideways instead of sliding. Hopping lifts both feet too high off the ground, leaving the receiver completely vulnerable if a defender jams him mid-air. Also: feet crossing rather than staying parallel.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver pushes off the front foot and slides the back foot sideways, feet staying wide and parallel and low to the ground, moving laterally to bypass the jam rather than through it.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees straightening or wobbling during the hesitation, so the receiver loses balance on the wide base or unloads the legs before the transition.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees stay deep and stable through the pause, absorbing the lateral momentum and holding balance on the wide base.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the pause, unloading the spring - the receiver then has to sink again before transitioning, which gives the defender time to recover.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay low and loaded through the hesitation, holding the compressed position so the forward transition can fire without a reset.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands hanging loose or away from the frame during the pause, giving the defender something to grab and leaving nothing loaded for the strike. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands retract tight to the lower ribcage into a compact ready position, loaded to strike as soon as contact comes.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning upfield during the hesitation, tipping the vertical release before the read is complete. (Gaze and the defender's reaction are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked forward on the defender through the pause, reading whether their hips open or freeze before the receiver commits to the vertical.

rows.fault_trigger: LEANING EARLY - tilting the head or shoulders toward the intended vertical route during the micro-pause, which completely tips off the true direction. Also: leaning back rather than forward, so no vertical threat is presented.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso tilts slightly forward over the toes to threaten an immediate vertical launch from the side lane, while the shoulders stay quiet and give nothing away.

rows.fault_trigger: Drifting through the hesitation rather than stopping cleanly, so there is no freeze for the defender to react to and the bait never lands.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The sliding foot plants firmly and the lateral movement stops dead for a fraction of a second, holding the wide base while the defender is frozen.

rows.fault_trigger: SOFT CLEAT PLANT - failing to slam the outside foot into the turf with force. A soft plant results in a slow, sluggish transition from horizontal to vertical, and the foot drifts rather than gripping.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside foot slams aggressively into the turf and grips, arresting all lateral momentum in one contact so it can be converted straight into forward drive.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning well before the plant (telegraphing the vertical) or lagging behind it, so the body commits before the receiver has picked up the lane. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head begins turning upfield toward the release lane as the plant lands, leading the body into the vertical transition.

rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff, straight leg, which cannot absorb the lateral force - the receiver slides through the plant or has to take a recovery step before going vertical.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee bends sharply - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - absorbing the lateral energy of the slide and converting it into straight-line power.

rows.fault_trigger: Staying square and upright through the plant, presenting a full chest just as the receiver commits and giving the defender a clean target to re-route.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder dips at the plant, lowering the chest profile and getting skinny against the defender's leverage as the transition begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying passive or low through the plant, leaving the receiver defenceless at the exact moment the defender is most likely to reach. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands come up fast into an aggressive strike position as the plant lands, ready to meet the defender if they reach out at the transition.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying level or rising at the plant instead of sinking, so nothing loads and the transition to vertical has no power behind it.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips sink further at the plant, loading the lower body so the lateral energy can be redirected into forward acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: DROPPING THE HANDS - letting the arms trail behind the body, leaving no protection against a recovering defender's arm bar or jersey pull. Also: an arm path that never clears the shoulder plane. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives violently past the shoulder plane - swipe, chop or club-rip - shattering the defender's reach as the receiver clears vertically.

rows.fault_trigger: Bursting through square-shouldered, leaving a full jersey surface exposed for a recovering defender to grab as the receiver passes.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away as the receiver bursts past, turning the chest off the defender and eliminating the jersey surface they could grab.

rows.fault_trigger: A slow or gradual push-off out of the plant, so the receiver never clears the defender's level and stays inside their reach as the route develops. (Defender position is not in frame - path and acceleration only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant foot drives explosively forward, accelerating the receiver past the defender's hip plane and clearing their level in one burst rather than easing into the route.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating slowly or only partway, leaving the receiver running at an angle across the field rather than vertically - the slide's advantage is lost in the transition.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips flip sharply from the lateral slide orientation to point straight upfield, locking the receiver onto the vertical track in a single decisive rotation.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the burst, so the first strides are short and shuffling and the receiver takes too long to reach full speed after the transition.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives high out of the transition, taking immediate ground upfield and accelerating the receiver toward top speed.

rows.fault_trigger: Head still turned toward the slide side after the burst, or coming round slowly, so the receiver is late reading coverage and late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head comes fully round to track upfield along the route, re-establishing vision quickly so the receiver can process cushion and locate the ball.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying low or arriving late, so the receiver has nothing ready when the defender's hands come. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands come up quickly to chest height into a tight, relaxed ready position as the feet land - loaded to strike but not tense.

rows.fault_trigger: OVER-SPLITTING - landing far too wide, which locks up the hips so the receiver cannot push off to change direction. Also: feet leaving the ground at different times rather than together, or landing staggered instead of parallel.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both feet leave the ground at the same instant, the back foot snapping forward and the front foot back, landing parallel and wider than shoulder width to establish a balanced, uncommitted base.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying too straight to load the split, or weight settling back onto the heels so the receiver cannot push off cleanly.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees bend deep into an athletic squat - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - with weight balanced evenly over the balls of the feet, ready to drive in any direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Head dropping to watch the feet during the split, losing sight of the defender at the moment the read has to happen. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked on the defender's belt line through the split, with no downward dip toward the feet as the body resets.

rows.fault_trigger: Landing tall and sinking afterwards, so there is a moment where the receiver is upright and unloaded - the split buys no advantage if the hips arrive late.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop the instant the feet land, lowering the centre of gravity immediately so the base is established and loaded in a single motion.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating during the split, which tips the release direction before the receiver has even read the defender.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay perfectly square to the defender through the split, with the torso leaning slightly forward over the knees to shield the chest.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the hesitation, unloading the base - the receiver then has to re-sink before moving, which costs the advantage the split created.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay low through the read, preserving the loaded position so the receiver can explode in whichever direction the defender opens.

rows.fault_trigger: LEANING EARLY - tilting the head or shoulders toward the intended release during the micro-pause, which completely tips off the true direction and wastes the freeze.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Quiet shoulders - no tilt, no rotation, no lean. The upper body gives away nothing while the receiver reads which way the defender is going.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees straightening during the hesitation, so the springs unload and the drive-off has to start from scratch.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees hold their deep flexion through the read - loaded springs, ready to extend the instant the defender commits.

rows.fault_trigger: RUSHING THE READ - turning the head toward the intended path before the defender has declared, or skipping the read entirely and committing blind. (Gaze and the defender's reaction are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked on the defender's midsection through the read, processing whether they freeze, lean, or slide before the receiver commits.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping or going passive during the hesitation, leaving the receiver with nothing ready when the jam arrives. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay up at chest level and active through the read, ready to strike the moment the defender's hands come.

rows.fault_trigger: Feet shuffling, creeping or resetting during the read, which breaks the freeze and tells the defender a move is coming.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The feet stay planted wide and parallel through the read - completely still, holding the base while the defender is frozen.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening slowly or lagging behind the plant, so the drive has no rotational force behind it and the receiver pushes sideways instead of exploding through the lane.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips turn and open violently toward the chosen lane the instant the plant foot hits, converting the loaded base into directional drive.

rows.fault_trigger: Driving into the lane square-shouldered and upright, presenting a full chest for the defender to get hands on and re-route the release.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The leading shoulder dips into the direction of the release - getting skinny - so the receiver presents the smallest possible target as he attacks the lane.

rows.fault_trigger: CLICK-BACK - dragging the driving foot instead of slamming it cleanly into the turf, which bleeds away the explosive power. Also: the foot sliding at contact rather than gripping.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The foot opposite the intended path slams cleanly into the turf with no slide, delivering full force to drive the body laterally and forward into the open lane.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying passive through the drive, leaving the defender free to land a clean jam on a receiver who is already committed to a direction. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands fire up and forward as the plant lands - striking, clearing or bypassing the defender's jam in the same instant the body drives.

rows.fault_trigger: Drive leg failing to extend fully, leaving force in the ground; or the lead knee not driving through, so the first stride out of the plant is short.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The drive leg extends fully to deliver every bit of force, while the lead knee flexes and drives forward to take immediate ground into the lane.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning before the plant (telegraphing the direction) or well after it (leaving the receiver driving blind into the lane). (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps toward the chosen attack path as the plant fires, committing the whole body to the direction in one motion.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips never finishing their rotation, leaving the receiver running at an angle across the field rather than vertically, which costs separation and distorts the route.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate fully to point straight downfield, locking the receiver onto the vertical track so the route can develop at full speed.

rows.fault_trigger: DROPPING THE HANDS - letting the arms trail behind the body, leaving no protection against a recovering defender's arm bar or jersey pull. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives sharply past the shoulder plane with a swift chop, clearing the defender's frame as the receiver locks onto the vertical track.

rows.fault_trigger: SLAMMING INTO THE DB - releasing directly into the defender's body instead of taking an angled, tight path past their hip. The aim is to clear their frame, not initiate a collision. Also: drifting wide of the track and losing ground. (Defender position is not in frame - path tightness only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The escape step drives straight upfield on a tight angled path past the defender's hip, clearing their level entirely rather than drifting wide or running into them.

rows.fault_trigger: Head staying turned toward the release side after the escape, or coming round slowly, so the receiver is late reading coverage and late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head comes round to track straight upfield, re-establishing vision quickly so the receiver can read coverage depth and locate the football.

rows.fault_trigger: Escaping square-shouldered, leaving a full jersey surface exposed for a trailing defender to grab or arm-bar.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing shoulder rolls inward and away as the receiver clears, eliminating the jersey surface a recovering defender could grab.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the escape, so the first strides are short and shuffling and the receiver takes too long to reach full speed.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high through the escape strides, building linear speed immediately and creating separation from the defender.

rows.fault_trigger: Knee lift dropping off during the stem, which slows the receiver and signals that he is preparing to break rather than running deep.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front knee lifts high through the swing phase on every stride, sustaining genuine top-end speed down the stem.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning toward the break direction during the stem, tipping the route before the receiver has reached the break point. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked straight downfield through the stem, selling the vertical route and giving the defender nothing to read.

rows.fault_trigger: Velocity dropping off during the stem, or excessive vertical bounce wasting energy - either way the deep threat is not sold and the defender does not have to respect it.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips carry constant high-speed forward travel with minimal vertical bounce - all the energy goes into covering ground down the stem.

rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump shortening or slowing during the stem, an early visual tell that the receiver is about to break.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump at full amplitude past the ribcage throughout the stem, driving the sprint and giving no indication a break is coming.

rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the stem, which reads as a receiver preparing to stop rather than one running past the defender.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds an aggressive forward lean over the toes through the stem, matching what a genuine deep sprint looks like.

rows.fault_trigger: STUTTER STEPPING - stride length shortening or step frequency rising before the break point, which tells the defender a cut is coming and surrenders the advantage the stem was built to create.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length stays maximal and constant through the vertical stem - the receiver runs at genuine top speed so the deep route is believable right up to the break.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders starting to rotate toward the break during the load step, an early tell that lets the defender jump the route.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay completely square to the stem and forward over the knees during the load - the upper body reveals nothing while the lower body prepares.

rows.fault_trigger: POPPING UP - a sudden upward spike in hip or chest height, destroying the low sprint angle and broadcasting the break. Also: sinking so far that forward velocity drops and the cut becomes a gather.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop a small, controlled amount to load the cut - without losing any forward speed. The sink is subtle enough that the defender cannot see it coming.

rows.fault_trigger: Arm mechanics changing during the load step - shortening, tightening or breaking rhythm - which gives the defender a visual cue that the break is imminent.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arm pump continues exactly as it was through the stem - unchanged amplitude and rhythm, so nothing about the upper body signals the load.

rows.fault_trigger: Stride shortening on the load step, which is a visible gather and tells the defender the break is one step away.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length holds at its full stem value through the load step while the weight quietly prepares to transfer laterally - nothing shortens or gathers.

rows.fault_trigger: Lead knee staying stiff through the load step, so the sink cannot be absorbed and the receiver either pops up or loses balance going into the plant.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee bends more deeply on the load step, absorbing the downward force of the sink while keeping the receiver stable at full speed.

rows.fault_trigger: Head beginning to turn during the load step rather than at the transition, breaking the deception one step too early. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays fixed downfield right through the load step, holding the deep threat until the exact frame the transition begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders lagging behind the head turn or staying square, so the upper body does not lead the cut and the transition has to be driven entirely by the plant.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders turn in time with the head, tilting into the new direction so the upper body initiates the cut and blindsides the defender before the feet move.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the bait, so the receiver arrives at the plant unloaded and cannot absorb the lateral force - the cut slips or rounds.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees stay actively bent through the bait, loaded and ready to handle the high-speed lateral shift that the plant is about to demand.

rows.fault_trigger: Feet drifting off the stem line during the bait, so the lower body commits before the plant and the cut loses its sharpness.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The feet keep tracking straight under the body along the stem while the upper body begins to turn - the lower body has not yet committed to the break.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating fully before the plant, committing early and letting the defender break on the route; or not uncoiling at all, so the plant has to do all the work and the cut rounds off.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips begin to uncoil toward the break direction, starting the rotation that the plant will complete.
