rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying wide through the bait, slowing the rotation and costing the receiver time in the break. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pull in tight to the body as the turn begins, tightening the frame so the receiver can rotate faster into the break.

rows.fault_trigger: BLIND TURNING - head yaw lagging behind the hip and shoulder rotation, meaning the receiver is turning blind rather than leading with his eyes, and will be late seeing the ball. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps hard and fast toward the new route trajectory, leading the whole movement - the eyes get there first and the body follows.

rows.fault_trigger: Staying upright through the plant, so momentum carries the receiver wide and the cut rounds off; or over-leaning and losing balance out of the break.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso tilts sharply inward toward the new route angle at the plant, countering the centrifugal force of the cut and keeping the receiver balanced through the turn.

rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff leg, which cannot absorb the speed or store energy - the receiver either slides through the cut or has to take recovery steps before accelerating.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant knee drops into deep flexion at contact, loading the leg as a high-speed spring that will fire the receiver out on the new line.

rows.fault_trigger: THE BLIND PLANT - the foot lands still pointing straight downfield instead of along the new path, so the receiver slides outward, loses his base, and the cut becomes a skid rather than a redirect. Toe left down (plantarflexed) rather than pulled up, so the receiver slides through the plant or stubs the toe instead of biting the ground heel-first. Over-extending or lunging the plant step out ahead of the centre of mass, which costs body control and tips the break early.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside cutting foot lands with the toe already pointed along the new route path, steering the body into the break rather than braking against it. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion so the heel bites the grass first, giving clean, firm contact instead of a slide or a stubbed toe. The step stays compact and lands directly beneath the centre of mass - no over-extending or lunging - which preserves body control and keeps the defender believing the receiver is still running vertically until the instant the weight drops.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening to a different angle than the head and plant foot, so the body fights itself through the cut and the exit line is wrong.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips snap open to exactly the angle the head and the plant foot have already established - head, foot and hips all pointing down the same new route line.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms flying wide at the plant, slowing the rotation and costing time in the break - and often unbalancing the receiver as he exits. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms stay tucked tight to the chest through the plant, keeping the frame compact so the body rotates as fast as possible into the new direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Head still rotating at the plant rather than already locked on the new corridor, so the receiver comes out of the cut late to find the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: By the plant the head is fully locked down the new route corridor, already looking for open space and the football before the body has finished turning.

rows.fault_trigger: A gather or recovery step between the plant and the first driving step, or the step drifting off the new line - either way the separation the cut created is handed straight back.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside foot drives immediately along the new route line with no drift, no gather step and no wasted movement between the plant and the acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying tucked or pumping weakly out of the cut, so the upper body contributes nothing to rebuilding speed on the new line.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms fire back into a violent forward pump the moment the cut is made, mechanically driving the receiver back up to sprinting speed.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning so far to track the ball that the body follows and drifts off the route line, or losing the target entirely coming out of the break. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head tracks the target while staying aligned with the new running lane - the receiver finds the ball without letting his body drift off the route line.

rows.fault_trigger: ROUNDING THE ANGLE - the pelvis trajectory forms a wide curve instead of a sharp linear exit, giving the defender time and space to recover the separation the cut had created.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips travel on a strict straight line along the new route path, exiting the cut at a sharp angle rather than curving out of it.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying rotated or the torso staying upright after the cut, so the receiver runs out of the break unbalanced and slow to rebuild speed.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders square up to the new route line and the torso resumes its forward sprinting lean, the body reset into pure acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the break, so the receiver shuffles back up to speed and the window the cut opened closes before the ball arrives.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives high and forward out of the cut, generating maximum instant acceleration back to full speed on the new line.

rows.fault_trigger: Knee drive dropping off during the stem, slowing the receiver early and removing the vertical threat the stop cut depends on.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The knees drive at full sprint height through the stem, generating the maximum speed that the breakdown will then have to absorb.

rows.fault_trigger: TELEGRAPHING - stride shortening or velocity dropping before the breakdown, which warns the defender the receiver is about to stop and lets them sit on the route.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length stays maximal through the vertical stem, holding genuine top speed so the deep threat forces the defender to turn and run.

rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump shortening or slowing during the stem, a visual tell that the receiver is about to break down.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump violently through the stem at full sprint amplitude, driving the vertical push and giving no hint the break is coming.

rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the stem, an early tell that the receiver is preparing to break down.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds an aggressive forward sprint lean through the stem, the posture of a receiver running past the defender rather than one preparing to stop.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning toward the break during the stem, breaking the vertical threat before the receiver has reached the break point. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked straight downfield through the stem, maintaining the deep vertical threat that makes the stop work.

rows.fault_trigger: Velocity easing off during the stem, so the deep threat is never established and the defender does not have to respect it.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips carry constant high-speed travel down the stem with minimal bounce, selling the vertical route before anything changes.

rows.fault_trigger: STIFF LEG - entering the breakdown with the hips still high, so the deceleration is absorbed through the knees rather than the whole lower body. Slower to stop and hard on the joints.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop drastically on the breakdown steps, dumping the centre of gravity low so the legs can absorb the speed and the body can anchor.

rows.fault_trigger: Too many chop steps, or a gradual slow-down rather than a sharp gather - the breakdown takes too long and the defender closes the space before the break.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride shortens rapidly into 2 to 3 chop steps, gathering the feet underneath the body to kill momentum in as little ground as possible.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying out over the toes through the breakdown, so momentum carries the chest forward and the receiver cannot stop cleanly or has to take recovery steps.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The forward sprint lean shifts back into a tucked, balanced position with the shoulders inside the knee frame, so the receiver can anchor rather than being carried forward.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying relatively straight through the breakdown, so there is nothing to absorb the momentum - the receiver skids, stumbles, or needs extra steps to stop.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees move from maximum sprint drive into deep bilateral flexion, working as shock absorbers to soak up the speed the stem built.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning during the breakdown rather than at the visual snap, giving the defender an extra beat of warning before the break. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked downfield through the breakdown steps, holding the deep threat even as the body gathers to stop.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms still swinging wide through the breakdown, throwing the receiver off balance at exactly the moment he needs to be stable. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The violent sprint pump compacts into a tight position near the chest, quieting the arms so they do not fight the deceleration or unbalance the body.

rows.fault_trigger: Still carrying forward velocity through the pause, so the receiver drifts past the break point and the route depth is wrong; or the base narrowing and losing the platform for the plant.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The wide, low stance holds for a beat as forward velocity reaches zero - the receiver is genuinely stopped, not still drifting.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the pause, unloading the legs - the receiver then has to drop again before he can drive out, and the break is late.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips hold their low position through the pause, staying loaded so the plant can fire without needing to re-sink.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating before or without the head, so the body commits blind and the receiver is late picking up the ball out of the break.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders rotate in behind the head turn, shifting the body's equilibrium toward the new break so the plant can redirect immediately.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping or going wide during the pause, so the receiver is neither ready for a quick throw nor compact enough to turn fast. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay elevated and active in a compact frame through the pause, ready to catch and tight enough not to slow the rotation.

rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the pause, so the stored energy leaks away and the drive out has to be generated from scratch.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The deep knee bend is maintained through the pause, keeping the lower body loaded like a spring ready to fire on the plant.

rows.fault_trigger: BLIND TURN - the torso rotates before the eyes do, so the receiver comes out of the break without having found the ball and is late reacting to a throw already in the air. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps immediately and fast toward the new route, leading the movement so the eyes find the quarterback before the body has finished turning.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders sitting back behind the plant foot, so the weight is behind the anchor and the receiver slips backward instead of driving out.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso leans securely out over the planting toe, keeping the weight stacked over the anchor so the receiver does not slip backward off the plant.

rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a straight or shallow-bent leg, which cannot absorb the remaining momentum - the receiver skids through the break or jars to a stop with nothing stored for the exit.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee flexes deep at contact, building a powerful stopping platform that absorbs the last of the momentum and stores it for the drive out.

rows.fault_trigger: BLIND PLANT - the toe points straight ahead or wide of the new path, so the foot brakes instead of steering and the receiver slips off the anchor. Toe left down (plantarflexed) rather than pulled up, so the receiver slides through the plant or stubs the toe instead of biting the ground heel-first. Over-extending or lunging the plant step out ahead of the centre of mass, which costs body control and tips the break early by showing the defender the receiver is gathering rather than still running.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside foot lands with the toe pointing exactly down the new route angle, acting as a steering mechanism rather than just a brake. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion so the heel bites the grass first, giving clean, firm contact instead of a slide or a stubbed toe. The step stays compact and lands directly beneath the centre of mass - no over-extending or lunging - which both preserves body control and keeps the defender believing the receiver is still accelerating vertically until the instant the weight drops.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips already rising at the plant rather than bottoming out, so the anchor is weak and the receiver gets carried past the break point.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips reach their lowest point of the entire cut at the plant - the core locked down against the ground, giving the anchor maximum stability.

rows.fault_trigger: Head snap arriving before or after cleat impact rather than with it - either the receiver tips the break early, or he is still turning when the ball is already on its way.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snap lands on exactly the same instant as the cleat hits the ground - eyes and anchor arriving together, so the receiver is looking at the quarterback the moment he is able to catch.

rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying compact or pumping weakly out of the break, so the upper body adds nothing to rebuilding speed from a dead stop - where it matters most.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms fire back into a violent punch-like pump the instant the drive out begins, mechanically restoring sprint momentum from a standing stop.

rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the break, so the receiver shuffles back up to speed and the throwing window closes before he can separate.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives immediately up and forward out of the plant, converting the stored energy into instant acceleration on the new line.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying rotated or the torso staying upright and tucked after the break, so the receiver runs out slow and unbalanced on the new line.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders square up to the new path and the torso resumes its forward sprint lean, the body reset from stopping posture into pure acceleration.

rows.fault_trigger: ROUNDING - the exit trajectory curves rather than forming a sharp line, so the defender recovers the ground the stop had won. Usually caused by the hips rotating too slowly out of the plant.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate rapidly to sit parallel with the new exit trajectory, locking the receiver onto a sharp straight line out of the break.

rows.fault_trigger: A gather step between the plant and the drive out, or a high, short first step - either way the stored energy is wasted and the defender recovers the separation the stop created.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The receiver pushes explosively off the instep of the plant foot into a low, linear first step - the anchor converts straight into acceleration with nothing wasted.

rows.fault_trigger: Losing the quarterback coming out of the break, or turning the head so far that the body follows and the exit line curves off the route. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked on the quarterback through the drive out, tracking the throw while the body holds its line on the new trajectory.

rows.fault_trigger: STIFF-LEGGED BRAKING - trying to stop without sinking the hips. The receiver stumbles forward, takes too many recovery steps, and puts dangerous stress on the knees. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the declared route.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the line and sprint at full vertical velocity for 12-15 yards, forcing the defender to turn their hips into a deep, desperate retreat. At break depth, violently sink the hips and chop the cleats rapidly into the turf - the sudden lowering of the centre of gravity is the braking system that halts forward momentum.

rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round late or after the body has pivoted, so the receiver finishes the break without having found the quarterback - and a ball already in the air arrives before he is looking for it. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The millisecond forward momentum halts, snap the head and eyes back around over the inside shoulder to face the quarterback first. Turning the vision inside opens the upper torso and picks up the ball's trajectory before the lower body has finished its pivot.

rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING TOE PLANT - reaching too far forward with the planting step and letting the toe point downward before contact. This strips core stability, causes a slide, and tips off the defender early because the running stride visibly changes before the cut.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes find the quarterback, drive the outside cutting foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the hips. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking heel and midfoot first to lock the brakes instantly. Pivot and direct the toe at a 45-degree angle back down the stem toward the sideline.

rows.fault_trigger: WAITING ON THE BALL - standing still after making the cut. The receiver must actively run back downhill toward the ball to stop a trailing defender undercutting the route for an interception. (Ball position and defender leverage are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot and work back downhill toward the ball, shortening the distance of the throw, squaring the shoulders to the quarterback to shield the ball, and securing the catch with the hands extended away from the frame.

rows.fault_trigger: FADING EARLY - unconsciously drifting outward toward the sideline before the break depth, alerting the defender to clamp down on the corner. Also: chopping or stutter-stepping into the load, which turns a speed cut into a visible breakdown. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the called depth.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive off the line at full velocity for 10-12 yards (12-15 on the deeper variation) with pads leaning forward and long natural strides, pushing the defender into a deep vertical retreat. One step before the break, subtly drop the hips an inch to gather balance and prepare the core for high-speed redirection - without chopping or stutter-stepping.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with the plant or after it rather than leading it, so the torso never pre-rotates and the break is slower and squarer than it should be. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At break depth, snap the head and eyes sharply toward the corner pylon first. The rapid visual rotation opens the upper torso and shifts equilibrium toward the outside before the lower body begins to pivot.

rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING SLIDE - lunging too far forward with a loose, downward-pointing toe. The over-extension lacks the rigidity to anchor a 45-degree turn, so the shoe slides over the grass and the defender closes the gap.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes lock onto the pylon, drive the INSIDE foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the centre of mass. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking with a rigid foot. Instantly point the toe down a 45-degree track toward the corner, masking the break until the last possible instant.

rows.fault_trigger: FLATTENING THE ANGLE - letting the route angle flat toward the sideline rather than holding a strict 45 degrees toward the corner pylon, which shortens the route and lets the defender close.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Push violently off the inside instep of the directing foot, flip the hips wide open, and punch the outside arm across the body to accelerate along a strict 45-degree line toward the corner.

rows.fault_trigger: FADING EARLY - drifting inward toward the middle of the field right off the snap. This tells the defender exactly where the receiver is going and lets them squeeze him into the linebacker level. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode vertically off the line for 2 to 3 hard steps, driving the pads forward to threaten the defender's leverage and make them respect the go route. Then prepare to redirect sideways by subtly sinking the hips, keeping the feet moving at full speed with no choppy or gathering steps.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with the plant or after it rather than leading it, so the shoulders never uncoil into the lane and the receiver crosses without having seen the linebacker level. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At break depth, snap the head and eyes sharply across the formation first. The visual focus locks onto the open grass underneath the linebackers, which naturally uncoils the neck and shoulders into the cross lane.

rows.fault_trigger: THE DOWNFIELD TOE PLANT - planting with the toe still pointing toward the end zone. Failing to direct the foot at 90 degrees causes the receiver to drift downfield, running straight into the waiting linebackers.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The instant the eyes find the cross lane, drive the outside foot down into a sharp, compact step positioned firmly beneath the body weight. The toe is pulled up before the foot strikes to ground cleanly. Instantly point the toe and direct the final step down a flat 90-degree track across the field, masking the horizontal break until the last possible instant.

rows.fault_trigger: BUBBLING THE ROUTE - letting the route angle backward toward the line of scrimmage or bubble downfield. The line must stay flat and parallel to the line of scrimmage to maximise the open void. (Ball location needs ball tracking.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Push violently off the inside instep of the directing foot, sprint flat along the line across the formation, snap the eyes back over the inside shoulder to look for the ball, and secure the catch while bracing to turn upfield.

rows.fault_trigger: TELEGRAPHING THE STOP - slowing down or rising out of the low pad level a couple of yards before the break point, which lets the defender instantly close the cushion. STIFF-LEGGED BRAKING - trying to stop without sinking the hips, causing a stumble, extra recovery steps, and dangerous stress on the knees.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the ball and sprint at full vertical velocity to roughly 12 yards, holding a low pad level and natural full strides to drive the defender into a deep backpedal. At break depth, violently sink the hips and chop the cleats rapidly into the turf - the sudden lowering of the centre of gravity is the braking system that halts the momentum the longer stem has built.

rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round late or after the body has pivoted, so the receiver finishes the break without having found the quarterback - and a ball already in the air arrives before he is looking for it. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: The millisecond forward momentum halts, snap the head and eyes back around over the inside shoulder to face the quarterback first. Turning the vision inside opens the upper torso and picks up the ball's trajectory before the lower body has finished its pivot.

rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING TOE PLANT - reaching too far forward with the planting step and letting the toe point downward before contact. This strips core stability, causes a slide, and tips off the defender early because the running stride visibly changes before the cut.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes find the quarterback, drive the cutting foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the hips. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking with a rigid foot to lock the brakes instantly. Pivot and direct the toe back down the stem toward the line of scrimmage, holding the illusion of a forward sprint until the exact moment of the cut.

rows.fault_trigger: WAITING ON THE BALL - standing still after making the cut. The receiver must actively run back downhill toward the ball to stop a trailing defender undercutting the route for an interception. (Ball position and defender leverage are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot, open the chest completely to the quarterback, work back downhill toward the ball to shorten the distance of the throw, and secure the catch with the hands extended away from the frame.

rows.fault_trigger: BANANA STEMMING - curving the path inward before making the actual break. A rounded line lets an inside-shade defender stay in front of the receiver the whole way. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the declared route.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Run an ultra-aggressive vertical stem for 12-15 yards, pushing directly at the defender's midsection to freeze their leverage and force a deep backpedal respecting the post or go. At break depth, violently drop the weight into the hips and chop the cleats heavily through a 3-step breakdown to absorb the extra momentum the longer stem has built.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with or after the plant rather than leading it, so the receiver breaks into the middle without having cleared his vision for crashing inside defenders. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At the absolute peak of the breakdown, snap the head and eyes around to face the quarterback first. The visual snap opens the torso and clears vision to read the inside linebackers before the body commits.

rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING THE BREAK - reaching too far inside with a long, diving step. This elongates the body frame, tells the defender exactly when the break is coming, and locks up the hips so the receiver cannot accelerate smoothly out of the cut. Also: THE FLOPPY-FOOT SLIDE - planting with a loose, downward-pointing toe out in front of the chest, lacking the rigidity to anchor a 90-degree turn, so the shoe slides over the grass.

The cleat slams down directly beneath the hips, instantly pointing the toe at a sharp 90-degree angle toward the middle of the field.

rows.fault_trigger: SLOWING DOWN FOR CONTACT - decelerating or stutter-stepping when an inside linebacker tries to reroute or jam. The receiver must sprint through the contact and use the hands to clear without dropping speed. (Defender contact is not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Pushing through the intermediate zone at 10-12 yards, expect a collision or squeeze from interior linebackers or safeties. Use a high-speed hand swipe, chop or arm bar to clear their contact while holding the vertical line without drifting off-track or losing a step.

rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING / FLOPPY FOOTWORK - reaching too far forward to try to outrun a deep safety, or running with a loose, downward-pointing toe. This strips core stability and caps top-end speed. Also: drifting laterally out of the void.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Squeeze tightly into the defensive void with the running track completely straight. Steps stay compact and directly beneath the centre of mass without overstriding, toes pulling up into sharp dorsiflexion on every stride for a rigid ankle lock, while the eyes track the ball over the inside shoulder.

rows.fault_trigger: EXPOSING THE BALL - catching with the body loose or waiting for the ball to hit the chest. Over the middle, failing to snatch with extended hands and instantly tuck results in drops and forced fumbles. (Ball position and contact are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Expect a heavy hit from a closing safety or linebacker over the middle. Keep the hands down late to mask the ball's arrival, then shoot the arms up violently to snap the ball out of the air at its highest point, instantly tucking it to protect against incoming contact.

rows.fault_trigger: BANANA STEMMING - curving the path inward before the actual break, letting an inside-shade defender stay in front the whole way. CHOPPING FEET - gathering or stutter-stepping before the break; a slant relies entirely on pure unmitigated speed, and chopping ruins the separation.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Fire off the line hard for 3 direct vertical strides in a fierce sprint-sell posture - the path must look identical to a go route to freeze the defender's feet and leverage. On the second step, subtly drop the hips an inch into a compact athletic posture while the feet keep moving at full velocity.

rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with or after the plant rather than leading it, so the receiver breaks across the defender's face without having cleared his vision - and on a route this quick, the ball is often already out. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: At the exact peak of the third stride, snap the head and eyes inside across the middle of the field first. The visual snap instantly clears vision to read the inside linebackers and pick up the ball's release.

The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion before impact to establish a firm ankle lock, and the step is not overextended. The cleat slams down directly beneath the hips, instantly directing the toe at a sharp 45 degrees toward the middle to slice across the defender's face without losing linear body control.

rows.fault_trigger: RUNNING FLAT - flattening the route out horizontally toward the opposite sideline. The receiver must hold a strict 45-degree angle to keep outrunning the trailing defender. (Ball location needs ball tracking.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Roll the body weight smoothly off the directing foot, punch the outside arm violently across the body to hold top sprinting speed, maintain the 45-degree trajectory, and catch the ball cleanly in stride.

rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotated away from the line before the snap, telegraphing the release direction to the defender, or shoulder line unlevel enough to unbalance the first step.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Shoulders remain controlled and aligned with the intended release position. The upper body should not rotate excessively away from the line before movement begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Front knee locked or straight, knee collapsing inside or outside the toe line, or rear knee too extended to contribute to the first movement.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Front knee is bent rather than locked. The knee tracks forward toward the toe while maintaining an athletic loaded position. Rear knee remains flexed enough to contribute to the first movement.

rows.fault_trigger: Head facing straight downfield rather than turned inside to the ball, or head unstable/bobbing pre-snap so the receiver reacts late. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only. Ball location needs ball tracking.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Head is turned inside toward the football before the snap, with eyes locked onto the ball. The receiver uses the football's movement as the visual snap cue rather than reacting to the quarterback's verbal cadence. Head position remains controlled and stable so the receiver can explode immediately when the ball is snapped without a false start.

rows.fault_trigger: Outside foot forward instead of the inside foot; stagger too deep or too shallow to release cleanly; front toe square or turned outward rather than slightly in; or the inward turn overdone so it pulls the hips inside and opens them before the snap. (Which foot is 'inside' depends on alignment side - not determinable from a solo clip.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Inside foot is forward, toward the ball. Feet maintain the appropriate stagger and orientation to allow the receiver to release without a false step. The front foot carries a very slight inward turn - enough to aid the release, but not so much that the turn carries up into the hips and opens them inside. The front foot supports the initial roll-off movement.

rows.fault_trigger: Swaying, rocking, or bouncing pre-snap rather than settling into a loaded position; or so rigid and locked that the first movement requires a reset. A false step at the snap is the downstream symptom.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Receiver remains stable but immediately movable. The stance is sufficiently loaded to prevent a false step while allowing explosive movement in the intended release direction.

rows.fault_trigger: Base too narrow to balance, or so wide it restricts the first step and forces a false step to recover.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Feet are approximately shoulder width apart, providing a stable and explosive base. The stance is wide enough for balance without restricting the first step.

rows.fault_trigger: Hands crossed over the body's midline, clamped tight to the torso, or held so low or high that the receiver cannot react to a press. Arms rigid rather than relaxed. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hands remain relaxed, uncrossed, and independent. Hands are positioned near the waist or slightly higher in front of the chest depending on anticipated coverage. Hands remain free to immediately react to a press defender.

rows.fault_trigger: Weight sitting back on the rear leg or evenly split, forcing a backward rock or false step before the release.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Approximately 70-80% of body weight is loaded onto the front leg. The rear leg remains available to contribute to the release. The receiver should be able to roll forward off the front foot without rocking backward or taking a false step.

rows.fault_trigger: Standing too tall with no forward readiness, or crouching so low the receiver cannot release cleanly. Chest behind or well past the front knee.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Chest and hips are lowered into an athletic position. The shoulders/chest are positioned over the front knee, creating forward readiness without excessive crouching.

rows.fault_trigger: Hips opened toward the release before movement begins, giving away direction, or hips drifting out from under the torso so the drive is weakened.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hips remain loaded underneath the torso and prepared to drive toward the release. Hips should not be excessively opened before movement begins.

rows.fault_trigger: Torso angle diverging from the shin angle - typically folding forward at the waist with the chest well ahead of the shin line, or standing the torso upright while the shin stays loaded, disconnecting upper and lower body.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Upper body is positioned at approximately the same forward angle as the loaded front shin, creating a connected lower- and upper-body position. Avoid excessive bending at the waist.

rows.fault_trigger: "Telegraphing the Cut". Lowering the pad level too early or staring at the defender's shins before launching, alerting them to brace or swim.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Aim your front shoulder directly at the thigh pad or knee line of the oncoming defender.

rows.fault_trigger: "Diving at the Ankles". Throwing the body too low or too early, allowing the defender to easily step over the block or swat the back down without breaking stride.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Launch horizontally across the defender's frame, physically throwing your body sideways.

rows.fault_trigger: Leading with the Head. Launching head-first into a defender's knees, creating a dangerous risk for neck and concussive injuries.
rows.ideal_execution_standard: Ensure the back or side of your shoulder connects with their legs to force the takedown.
Keep the head up and eyes locked entirely on the target through the entirety of the strike to protect the neck.
